question: Re-fetch the current UT Lesson 2 and test SKILL's separation of Akkadogram IṢ-BAT from Hittite reading ēpta and copy horizon from cult provenance. Which actual passage remains visible, and which Hattic genealogy legs are still unsupported by this page?
source_locator: UT Hittite Online, Lesson 2, 'The Telepenus "Vanishing God" Myth (Anatolian mythology)', by Sara E. Kimball and Jonathan Slocum: commentary opening paragraph; 'Reading and Textual Analysis' first paragraph; interlinear gloss notes for IṢ-BAT (mist/windows and smoke/house clauses), Ú-UL (three clauses), and DUTU-us (Great Sun God clause); 'Lesson Text' and 'Translation' blocks follow
source_excerpt: IṢ-BAT -- verb; Akkadogram 3rd person singular preterite of ṣabātu seize, take -- seized # The Hittite reading is ēpta.
retrieval_method: Direct live HTTP fetch of the public UT Austin Linguistics Research Center page via FetchURL on 2026-10-17 (round-7 re-check, not a copy of the round-6 record); full extracted English page text read from the tool output; quotations copied verbatim from this retrieval; Hittite forms are the page's romanized transliteration with English interlinear gloss; Akkadograms/Sumerograms appear in editorial sign spelling as published.
basis: Live re-fetch on 2026-10-17 confirms the page is still reachable and the target passages remain visible. (1) Written-versus-read separation re-verified: the interlinear gloss still marks IṢ-BAT 'Akkadogram 3rd person singular preterite of ṣabātu seize, take -- seized' with the explicit note '# The Hittite reading is ēpta.', and this gloss pair occurs twice (mist seizing the windows; smoke seizing the house); three further clauses gloss Ú-UL as 'Akkadian negative ... not' with '# The Hittite reading is natta.' So the spelling (Akkadogram) is separable from the spoken Hittite reading on the live page, matching the entry's line 57 rejection (a logogram does not make the clause Akkadian) and its line 45 manuscript-chronology caution. (2) Copy horizon vs cult provenance kept separate: the copy-horizon sentence remains in 'Reading and Textual Analysis': 'The text exists in several copies, the earliest of which follows the writing conventions of the Middle Hittite period, but is probably a copy of an even earlier version.' This is a distinct variable from the cult-provenance statements in the commentary: 'Telepenus, son of the Hattic Stormgod, was a god of agriculture.' and 'played various roles in Hittite religious cult.' Supporting the entry's lines 45 (composition vs copy date) and 55 (inherited Hattic cult within Hittite settings) as separate layers. New substantive passage this round, not quoted in R6-05-A: the DUTU-us gloss states the reading 'is probably Istānus, from the name of the Hattic Sungod Estan' and that the myth 'is of Hattic origin' -- extending the same written-layer logic (Sumerogram DUTU + u-stem complement read as a Hittite name behind a Hattic solar deity name) and adding cult-provenance evidence for Hattic origin of the myth. Answer to the question's first half: the visible passages are the IṢ-BAT/ēpta glosses (twice), the copy-horizon sentence, and the Hattic-Stormgod / Istānus-Estan provenance lines. Verdict partial-support because the page re-verifies both separations while supporting none of the Hattic genealogy legs (see limits).
limits: Hattic genealogy legs unsupported by this page, as asked: the page nowhere states Hattic's non-Indo-European classification, nor any relation to North Caucasian or Yeniseian families, nor Hattic ancestry of Hittite; its 'of Hattic origin' is myth/cult provenance, not language genealogy. The entry's line-55 genealogical rejection therefore stays untested here (not contradicted, not supported), and this page must not be cited as establishing Hattic genealogy. The Hattic storm-god's native Hattic name (the entry's 'Taru') does not appear; the page says only 'Hattic Stormgod'. 'Istānus/Estan' is the authors' conjecture ('probably'), not a tablet reading. Medium is one English-language pedagogical secondary-scholarly page; no cuneiform autograph, no Hattic-language text, and no Hattic/Hittite bilingual tablet was read directly -- all Hattic content is mediated by the authors' English commentary. The page itself flags unclear items (marmarra-, immarni-, 'the meaning of the word is unclear'), and the DUTU-us reading is hedged. FetchURL flattened the page's expand-all gloss layout, so gloss-block formatting is reported from extracted text; absence of wording drift versus round 6 is observed only for the quoted passages, not certified for every byte of the page.
